paper_title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Rapid advances in video generation have improved the visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and realism of synthetic content, bringing new possibilities to media creation. The same progress makes fabricated recordings increasingly diﬀicult to distinguish from authentic ones, raising concerns over misinformation, impersonation, and public trust. Reliable AI-generated video detection is therefore becoming an essential component of media forensics, where decisive cues span visual, textual, and audio dimensions and call for role-specific inspection (Figure 1). To meet this need, recent studies [15, 18, 20, 23, 28, 30, 33, 34, 36, 4446, 56] use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) either to reason about authenticity in natural language or to coordinate expert analysis. However, as illustrated in Figure 12, these approaches still face two challenges in how forensic evidence is examined and used. a) Holistic single-pass reasoning. CoT-centric methods [20, 28, 36, 44, 45] judge the whole video in one pass, with one model covering every artifact type. Artifacts confined to brief interval or small region are easily missed or explained away by hallucinated rationales (Figure 6a), and claims entangled in one free-form trace cannot be checked or supervised individually. b) Static workflows or coordinator-only learning. Agent-based detectors either run fixed expert pipeline [17, 30, 46] or train only the coordinator over fixed specialists. ARGUS [56] collects four expert reports and freezes the observers while training the judge, so irrelevant reports can outweigh the one that finds the artifact (Figure 6b). Tool-augmented detectors [33, 47] instead learn when to invoke tools, yet keep tool backends fixed. Both remain bounded by the local accuracy of frozen sub-agents, since an inspector that misses subtle cue limits what better routing or aggregation can recover (Figure 6, right). To overcome these challenges, we introduce WeVisForensics (Figure 2), an agentic paradigm that couples adaptive evidence collection with self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents coordinated by main investigator agent along two complementary designs. 1) Adaptive forensic analysis. The Forensic Sub-agent Library (FSL) holds trainable inspectors that examine visual appearance, physical consistency, commonsense plausibility, and on-screen text, while audio tools inspect the soundtrack when one is present. Each call specifies forensic role and temporal scope, and the selected inspector returns findings that inform subsequent reasoning. The investigator uses these observations to request further inspections or issue an authenticity verdict, so evidence collection adapts to each video beyond predefined workflow. 2) 2 Investigator-inspector self-evolution. Adaptive dispatch still relies on what each inspector can detect, so the inspectors must also improve from the calls they serve. Yet because the investigator decides which inputs the inspectors encounter while their responses shape its decisions, updating both on every batch makes each moving target for the other. Our DTPO (Dual-Timescale Policy Optimization) therefore trains both from shared trajectories on two timescales (Figure 3). The investigators inspection policy is updated on every rollout batch using outcome rewards and call-level feedback. The inspectors accumulate the calls issued by the investigator, keep those grounded in annotated artifact intervals, select responses with interaction feedback for privileged distillation, revise their skill cards of reporting rules, and periodically refresh the FSL. The refined inspectors then return to subsequent rollouts, so the agent evolves from its own environment. Moreover, existing forensic video datasets [15, 20, 44] supervise single detector with verdict or holistic rationale, providing neither role-specific evidence for sub-agents nor trajectories for coordinating them. We therefore curate ForenCue-30K, which decomposes forensic supervision by role. Each record isolates one forensic perspective and specifies verdict, confidence, and the temporal interval of the artifact, so that sub-agent learns to report what its role can verify, including when the evidence is inconclusive. Agentic trajectories are assembled from executed sub-agent calls rather than imagined observations, so every decision is conditioned on evidence the main agent would actually receive. An accompanying RL pool supports DTPO. Since existing benchmarks score only the final verdict, we build AgenticCue, an agentic benchmark that groups generated videos by forensic category and evaluates both detection accuracy and whether an agent invokes the relevant sub-agents. Our contributions are threefold: We propose DTPO, an RL algorithm in which the investigator and its inspectors co-evolve from shared interactions on fast and slow timescales. Inspectors refine their weights and skill cards on the very calls the investigator issues, so its rollouts become their curriculum. We present WeVisForensics, an agentic video forensics framework in which main agent adaptively dispatches inspections to the FSL. The invocation strategy and sub-agent competence are jointly learned through DTPO. We curate ForenCue-30K, role-structured dataset with agentic trajectories covering diverse generators, and introduce AgenticCue, the first agentic forensic benchmark that evaluates both accuracy and call precision.

sections.title: 2 WeVisForensics Agent Framework
sections.content: WeVisForensics treats AI-generated video detection as an investigation rather than single act of perception. human forensic analyst rarely judges video from one glance: they form hypothesis from the overall content, zoom in on the moment and the region where it can be tested, consult the appropriate specialist, and keep collecting evidence until the conclusion is supported. WeVisForensics turns this workflow into an agent system with two levels. main agent, the investigator, plans the investigation, and Forensic Subagent Library (FSL) of inspectors examines the video from complementary forensic perspectives and returns structured evidence. The framework is built on three design principles. (i) Separation of planning and perception. The investigator decides what to check and where, while each inspector decides whether the artifact of its specialty is present in the requested scope. Planning thus scales with the complexity of video, and perception remains specialized and verifiable. (ii) Role-decomposed evidence. Every inspection returns verdict, calibrated confidence, and visibly grounded explanation for single forensic perspective. Each piece of evidence can therefore be audited, supervised, and credited on its own, instead of being entangled in one free-form rationale. (iii) Evolvable components. The parts of the system whose competence depends on the changing distribution of generators, namely the investigation policy and the visual inspectors, are trained to improve from the systems own interactions, whereas measurement-like tools stay fixed and provide stable reference. Sec. 2.1 specifies the investigation protocol, Sec. 2.2 describes each member of the FSL, and Sec. 4 presents the training pipeline. 3 Figure 3 WeVisForensics and its training strategy, DTPO. The investigator rolls out with fixed FSL snapshot and is updated on every batch with outcome rewards and CLUE. Grounded calls (DOPD) queue by role in the interaction pool, from which the slow process distills privileged EMA teachers into students, revises skill cards, and refreshes the FSL every steps. 2.

The appearance inspector checks texture stability under motion, the integrity of fine details and boundaries such as hair, fingers, teeth, and small objects, unexplained local changes in sharpness, ghosting or duplication, and the temporal and geometric consistency of lighting, shadows, and reflections. The physical inspector checks biological and kinematic motion, structural integrity of bodies and rigid objects, object permanence across occlusion, contact and grasping, and the dynamics of fluids and deformable materials. The investigator calls appearance and physical checks on most videos and reserves commonsense checks for overviews that suggest specific semantic or causal anomaly, such as an animal performing human task or an event whose outcome contradicts ordinary world knowledge. The investigator itself is optimized with reinforcement learning, so the system improves both in what it asks and in what it is told.

sections.title: 3.1 Role-Grounded Supervision Construction
sections.content: Supervision is constructed in pipeline that mirrors the structure of the agent (Figure 4). Each curated video is first annotated separately for every forensic role, the annotations are then converted into training records for the inspectors, and executed inspector calls are finally assembled into investigation trajectories for the investigator. Every stage keeps the same role taxonomy, so the evidence an inspector learns to report is exactly the evidence the investigator learns to request and interpret. Instead of one holistic rationale per video, supervision is organized by forensic Role-structured taxonomy. perspective and subdivided into fine-grained artifact dimensions. Matching the six FSL roles, we categorize artifacts into Visual appearance (26,378 records), Physical consistency (32,348), Common sense (40,246), OCR consistency (18,580), ASR analysis, and Audio profile. Visual appearance covers texture and detail integrity, boundary blending, ghosting, and the consistency of lighting, shadows, and reflections. Physical consistency covers body and object structure, kinematics, object permanence, contact, and fluid or deformable dynamics. Common sense covers causality, affordances, contextual roles, and event order, and OCR consistency covers glyph structure and the temporal stability of rendered text. The audio roles cover the plausibility of speech timing and the agreement between the voice and the visible speaker. Each record isolates one perspective and specifies verdict (issue, no-issue, or inconclusive), confidence, an explanation, and the temporal interval of the artifact. Real videos contribute records under the same format, so every role sees both outcomes. This balance teaches each inspector to report only what its role can verify, rather than to equate generated with an artifact of my type is visible. Evidence annotation. sections.title: 4 Training Pipeline
sections.content: WeVisForensics is trained in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on ForenCue-30K first teaches the investigator the investigation protocol and each inspector its role-specific reporting format (Sec. 4.1). DTPO then lets the investigator and the inspectors improve together from their own interactions (Sec. 4.2), and scalable implementation keeps the joint training practical (Sec. 4.3). Every model is adapted with low-rank adapters on shared backbone, so that the investigator and all inspectors can be loaded and served as one backbone plus few lightweight adapters, and both stages update every model in the same parameterization.

sections.title: 4.2 Stage II: DTPO
sections.content: DTPO makes interaction experience the link between learning to request evidence and refining the inspectors that provide it. sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Evaluation on standard benchmarks. Table 4 shows that WeVisForensics attains the strongest detection performance on both the in-domain and the out-of-domain benchmarks. On the in-domain split, binary detectors stay near chance, whereas MLLM-based detectors benefit from domain supervision, and WeVisForensics reaches 97.7%, surpassing VideoVeritas by 3.4% and ARGUS by 11.3%. On the out-of-domain splits, generic MLLMs suffer from low fake recall regardless of scale, and CoT detectors drop sharply across unseen generators. WeVisForensics ranks first on GenBuster++ at 97.5% and on the six-generator MintVid mean at 88.0%, improving over the SFT agent on every generator category, which demonstrates strong generalization to unseen generators. Evaluation on AgenticCue. The five categories of AgenticCue expose the blind spots of prior paradigms across artifact types. Generic MLLMs handle commonsense violations but miss fine-grained anomalies, as Qwen3.5-397B reaches 94.5% on commonsense but only 54.1% on audio. It should also distinguish merely fantastical subject matter from contradictions in the depicted event, such as unsupported objects, unexplained attachments, or actions that require impossible mechanics. The selected interval covers the transition from the close ground-level views to the wider airborne views, making it appropriate for evaluating the central causal claim without relying only on isolated visual artifacts. Sub-agent returns. issue (high). The scene depicts commercial passenger aircraft taking off from an airport runway while carrying large red sleigh filled with presents and Santa-like figure. The sleigh is positioned behind the aircraft and appears to travel with it, but no visible mechanism explains how the sleigh is attached, supported, or propelled. The aircrafts ordinary flight behavior is therefore combined with an unexplained passenger-carrying vehicle that has no plausible operational role in the scene. The Christmas trees and decorations fit festive theme, but they do not provide causal explanation for the sleighs movement or the aircrafts unusual load. The event is clearly visible across multiple frames, making the semantic and causal inconsistency suﬀiciently observable. Step 2 Main agent physical_consistency[9.4--15.1 s] Reasoning. The preceding semantic review identifies strong causal concern: the sleigh appears to accompany the aircraft without an evident explanation for its support or propulsion. That finding supports more focused physical examination, but it does not by itself establish whether the apparent motion is practical stunt, an edit, or generated imagery. The next useful test is therefore physical consistency across the same late sequence. This review should track the aircrafts trajectory, the sleighs position and orientation, the apparent connection between them, and whether their motion remains mechanically coherent as the camera perspective changes. It should also check for continuity in the aircrafts structure and the sleighs relationship to the surrounding airport environment. Because the available interval is sampled rather than continuous, the assessment should remain attentive to uncertainty about unseen attachment points, forces, and intermediate motion, while still determining whether the visible dynamics provide credible real-world explanation. Sub-agent returns. issue (high). The aircraft and sleigh do not maintain physically plausible contact or motion relationships. The sleigh appears to travel alongside and then behind the aircraft while remaining suspended above the tarmac, with no visible support, propulsion, or mechanically credible connection. Across the sequence, the aircraft rises and advances while the sleigh stays at similar height and follows separate path, despite the apparent proximity and alignment suggesting shared movement. The sleigh also passes close to the aircraft without clear collision response or consistent depth relationship. The reindeer antlers on the aircraft are visible, but they do not provide plausible mechanism for pulling or carrying the sleigh. These are clear violations of contact, trajectory, and object-motion consistency rather than ordinary camera movement or normal airport maneuver. Step 3 Main agent: final verdict answer(fake) Verdict. Both analyses independently identify high-confidence problems in the central event. The common-sense assessment finds that commercial passenger aircraft appears to take off while carrying or traveling with large red sleigh and Santa-like figure, but no visible mechanism explains how the sleigh is supported, attached, or propelled. The physical-consistency assessment reinforces this: the sleigh follows separate path while remaining at similar height, lacks credible contact or motion relationships, and passes near the aircraft without consistent depth or collision response. The antlers are decorative and do not supply plausible pulling mechanism. The festive decorations and airport setting are coherent in isolation, but they do not resolve the impossible load and motion. Although sampled frames leave some intermediate behavior unobserved, the repeated causal and physical contradictions across the interval are substantial. The media is therefore best classified as fake. Figure 9 Passenger aircraft and airborne sleigh in generated airport scene. Ground truth: fake; WeVisForensics prediction: fake; 16.0 s, with audio. sections.title: 6.1 AI-Generated Video Detection
sections.content: Early detectors treat the task as binary classification over generation traces in images [27, 35, 41, 43] and videos [2, 5, 13, 22, 54], outputting score without verifiable evidence, and benchmarks such as GVD [2], GenVideo [5], GenVidBench [26], and AIGVDBench [24] scale up binary evaluation across generators. Building on MLLM-based image forensics [12, 14, 21, 51, 53], recent video detectors pair each verdict with natural-language account of the observed artifacts. Methods such as BusterX [44], BusterX++ [45], and VidGuard-R1 [28] train this reasoning with reinforcement learning, while Skyra [20], VideoVeritas [36], and VidForensics-M1 [23] strengthen it with artifact grounding, perception pretext tasks, and temporal-grounding rewards, respectively. IVY-FAKE [15] and Omni-Fake [18] provide annotated data for explainable detection, while OmniVL-Guard [34] unifies detection and grounding across text, images, and videos. However, these detector-centered formulations do not learn when to request specialized follow-up inspection or how to adapt it to intermediate observations.

sections.title: 6.2 Agent-Based Forensic Reasoning
sections.content: General video agents query specialized models to gather evidence over long inputs [19, 42, 48], while forensic agents organize analysis through explicit tools or specialized roles. Tool-augmented detectors such as ClueAegis [4], OmniVL-Guard Pro [33], and TUE-Detector [47] train single MLLM to invoke specific toolchains or visual operations such as cropping, zooming, and segmentation. Multi-agent methods such as SafeGuard [46], Hermes [17], and DVAR [30] instead distribute evidence extraction, verification, and deliberation across specialized agents. ARGUS [56] and Deepfake-Agent [9] further train judge or aggregator over fixed expert agents. However, the invoked experts in these designs never learn from the interactions they serve while the coordinating policy is trained, leaving the experts forensic response policies outside the ongoing policy-learning loop.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper presents WeVisForensics, an agentic framework for AI-generated video detection in which an investigator coordinates self-evolving library of forensic inspectors. Within this framework, DTPO is introduced to optimize the investigator on fast timescale while refining the inspectors from its calls on slow one. To support training and evaluation, ForenCue-30K is constructed with role-specific supervision and executed trajectories, and AgenticCue is established to assess both detection verdicts and the inspections behind them. Extensive experiments across benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of WeVisForensics, highlighting the value of co-evolving the investigator with its inspectors.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Training and inference setup. The main agent and the four visual sub-agents are rank-64 LoRA adapters on shared Qwen3.5-4B backbone, initialized from SFT adapters trained on 33,896 interaction trajectories and 117,552 role-specific records, while the base Qwen3.5-4B serves as the frozen CLUE reference pref. The main agent observes up to 16 uniformly sampled frames of the full video, and each window-based visual sub-agent inspects its requested window at 2 FPS, whereas the OCR sub-agent inspects the frame at its requested timestamp and the two audio tools analyze the whole soundtrack in Sec. 2.2. In the fast process, GRPO samples G=4 rollouts per video with 32 videos per batch and at most 4 sub-agent calls per trajectory for one epoch over the RL pool, and the main-agent learning rate warms up linearly to 1105. CLUE uses ϵ=0.1 and b=1 in Eq. (10) and call-advantage weight λ=0.2, and the tool-coverage F1 bonus has weight 0.3. In the slow process, calls with utility below κ=0.05 are relabeled as hedges, and each visual sub-agents adapter is refreshed every H=20 main-agent steps on class-balanced batches of 32 grounded calls, with the sub-agent learning rate decayed linearly from 3105 over training progress, decision-token weight ω=5, label-correction weight β=1, and teacher EMA rate ρ=0.001. The audio tools remain fixed during training. AgenticCue composition and evaluation metrics. AgenticCue comprises 2,830 unique videos in total: 2,330 unique generated videos and 500 fixed real videos. Each of the five forensic categories (Visual, Physical, OCR, Common sense, and Audio) contains exactly 500 generated videos verified to exhibit that categorys artifact (170 generated videos carry annotations for more than one category, yielding 2,330 unique generated clips across the five 500-clip category sets). For category s, binary detection accuracy (Acc.s) is evaluated under balanced 1:1 pairing of its 500 generated videos and the 500 real videos (1,000 videos per category), counting invalid or missing outputs as errors. Sub-agent invocation precision (Prec.s) measures whether the agent calls the relevant tool for its artifact: computed at the video level over the full pool of generated videos, with Prec.s = Cs Gs/Cs where Cs is the set on which the agent invokes tool at least once and Gs is the set of videos that call for role s. Two label systems are involved. The 500-clip category membership above only defines the accuracy subsets, and clip assigned to one category can still exhibit artifacts of other roles. Gs for the four visual roles therefore comes from the dense role annotations of Section 5, where two cross-family VLM annotators independently mark every role worth inspecting on each generated video and label-blind judge resolves disagreements. Two videos without resolved annotation are excluded, leaving 2,328 eligible videos for the visual roles. These annotations do not cover audio, so Gs for audio is the 500-clip Audio category over all 2,330 generated videos. An agent that invokes tool on every eligible video attains the base rate Gs/eligible, which is 91.1%, 78.6%, 49.2%, 24.0%, and 21.5% for the appearance, physical, OCR, commonsense, and audio roles. Table 3 summarizes these label counts. Precision is read together with category accuracy, which would drop if the agent skipped relevant inspections. DTPO raises accuracy on every AgenticCue category  (Table 12)  , including OCR, commonsense, and audio.

sections.title: B Human Review of Annotations
sections.content: Role-specific evidence annotations and main-agent interaction trajectories are produced by model annotators and coupled with human feedback (Figure 4) before entering the training records of Section 3. During prompt development and source onboarding, human reviewers inspect sampled annotations per source and role, flagging hallucinated explanations, over-generalized commonsense claims, imprecise temporal windows, or redundant/omitted tool calls. These failure modes are fed back to refine the annotation prompts and filtering rules, while unplayable clips are discarded. For the audio role, reviewers work through per-source queue, watch each video with its audio, and record whether the soundtrack is inconsistent with the visible speech along with the offending interval (Figure 11a). Quantitative human audit of sub-agent annotations and main-agent trajectories. To quantify the quality of the resulting supervision in ForenCue-30K, we conduct two model-assisted human verification audits (fixed random seed 42), summarized in Figure 10: Sub-agent role annotations (Figure 10a): We audit 340 videorole annotations on 100 generated training videos across all four visual specialist roles (100 Visual appearance, 100 Physical consistency, 100 Common sense, and 40 OCR consistency on clips). Overall, 99.1% (337/340) of the role annotations are at least partially supported by visual evidence (94.7% [322/340] fully supported and 4.4% [15/340] partially correct), with only 0.9% (3/340) judged incorrect (99.0% supported on Visual, 99.0% on Physical, 100.0% on Common sense, and 97.5% on OCR). For each trajectory, the auditor watches the video with audio, inspects the sequence of invoked tools and returned observations, and judges whether the tool selection is appropriate or suffers from omitted or redundant role invocations. The pairs are stratified by role, video label, and verdict agreement. reviewer sees both responses in random order with model identities hidden (Figure 11b), marks which response gives more accurate evidence, and flags in each response unsupported or mislocalized claims and missed visible anomalies. second reviewer re-checks the judgments. The evolved sub-agents are preferred in 65 pairs against 20, and the share of responses with any flaw falls from 30.5% to 8.0%  (Table 10)  . sections.title: C Detailed Detection Results

sections.title: D Learned Skill Cards
sections.content: This section lists the complete skill cards learned by the forensic library across four training runs. Each rule is appended to the user prompt of the corresponding sub-agent alongside the inspection query. Report rules specify generation artifacts to flag, while Ignore rules describe benign camera, motion, or compression effects that should not be mistaken for synthesis errors. The learned rules are local and contrastive. typical Report rule describes an artifact against an intact reference in the same frame, such as single fused glyph among sharp neighboring characters or melting facial contours against sharp background, and the matching Ignore rule names the global degradation that produces similar look, such as uniform blur or compression across the whole region. Because each edit is mined from calls that the current inspector still judges wrongly, the cards are specific to the failures of that run and differ in concrete content across runs. For example, the physical card of Run 2 targets finger articulation and garment topology, whereas that of Run 3 targets rigid tools sliding over granular surfaces and morphing sculptures. Run

sections.title: E Additional Evolution Comparisons
sections.content: Figure 13 runs the three paradigms of Figure 12 on the same generated street-market clip. All three return fake, yet only the adaptive agent grounds its verdict in evidence that exists in the video. The CoT-based detector asserts that the subject moves backward between 0.0 and 3.0 and snaps into new pose at 3.5 s, neither of which happens. The fixed-workflow detector queries four preset observers in parallel, and its judge aggregates reports of an abrupt scene cut at 0.3 and floating lantern that are equally unsupported. WeVisForensics instead issues two targeted calls. An appearance call over [0.0, 8.0] finds that the emblem and yellow shapes on the red lantern change contour and placement across frames while its paper ridges stay regular, and it sets aside the soft background crowd as ordinary depth of field. An OCR call at 4.0 then separates the intact calligraphy of the main sign from localized glyph degradation on the apron text. Figure 12 Comparison of AI-generated video detection paradigms. a) CoT-based reasoning uses textual rationales. b) Multi-agent workflows follow fixed execution structures. c) WeVisForensics adaptively coordinates subagents and evolves them together with the main policy. Figure 14 isolates what evolution changes on generated showroom video. VideoVeritas takes the stable lighting and showroom background at face value and answers real. The ARGUS observers do mention airbrushed skin, unstable hand edges, and rigid hair, but these cues are diluted among generic summaries and the judge still answers real. Before and after DTPO, WeVisForensics opens with the same appearance call over [0, 4.1] s. The SFT sub-agent returns no_issue, follow-up voice-profile check finds no anomaly, and the agent answers real. The evolved sub-agent returns issue on the identical call, locating soft and indistinct hand and finger boundaries as the speaker extends both arms. The main agent follows up with physical-consistency check rather than an audio tool and answers fake. Sharper evidence on the same first query thus reverses the verdict and redirects the rest of the investigation. 33 Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of investigation paradigms. All three approaches classify the generated video as fake. The CoT-based detector makes unsupported motion claims, and the fixed-workflow detector aggregates predefined observer reports. The adaptive agent requests localized appearance and OCR inspections and grounds its verdict in changing emblem contours and degraded apron lettering. Figure 14 Complete evolution comparison. On an AI-generated video, the CoT-based VideoVeritas and the fixed-workflow ARGUS both answer real. Before DTPO (top right), the appearance sub-agent reports no issue and WeVisForensics answers real. After DTPO (bottom right), the same first inspection localizes soft hand and finger boundaries during the opening gesture, and the main agent answers fake.

sections.title: F Additional Inspection Examples
sections.content: Figures 1517 give three further complete investigations in the format of Section 5.6, covering appearance, physical, commonsense, and OCR evidence on generated videos and real recording. 34 Investigation trace: garbled product label Step 1 Main agent visual_appearance[0.0--5.0 s] Reasoning. The sequence shows one apparent presenter demonstrating cosmetic bottle in retail-like setting, with the camera moving from wider view toward close view. The main hypothesis is that the media may be synthetic if fine details fail to remain stable during this motion, especially on the bottle, dropper, hands, face, and background display. full-range visual appearance inspection is therefore the most useful first step: it can compare object boundaries, textures, and local details across the entire five-second interval rather than relying on single frame. This scope also helps distinguish ordinary motion blur or changing perspective from details that appear to regenerate or deform. The result should establish whether there is broad temporal appearance concern and identify any specific regions that warrant more targeted physical or text-focused examination. Sub-agent returns. issue (medium). The clearest appearance concern is the unusually smooth, rendered quality of the womans face during the close-up application sequence. Across the cheek, nose, and jaw, the skin has broad, nearly textureless tonal gradients, while the eyelashes, lip outline, ear, and nearby bottle edges remain comparatively crisp. The cheek droplets also appear as clean, rounded highlights against this uniformly softened surface. This combination gives the face waxy, synthetic appearance rather than simply making the entire image soft. The effect persists as her hand moves across the cheek, making it more than an isolated blurred view. Confidence is medium because cosmetic smoothing and image processing can produce similar cues, and the frames do not establish separate, unmistakable boundary failure. Step 2 Main agent physical_consistency[0.0--5.0 s] Reasoning. The preceding appearance review raises possible synthetic-rendering concern, but that concern is not by itself decisive because cosmetic smoothing, lighting, and compression can create similar visual effects. The next question is whether the depicted action obeys ordinary physical continuity. The presenter handles bottle, raises dropper, and brings liquid toward her face, so the full five-second interval should be checked for stable hand anatomy, plausible contact, consistent object motion, and coherent liquid behavior. physical-consistency analysis over the same range is useful because it can either provide independent support for the appearance concern or reveal that the motion remains plausible despite visual stylization. The available one-second overview is sparse, so this check should be interpreted with appropriate caution, particularly around the exact moment of dropper contact and any brief transitions between sampled frames. Sub-agent returns. issue (medium). The woman holds dropper above an open bottle and then brings it toward her face. In the close views, the dropper tip and the small amount of liquid on her cheek are visible, but the frames do not clearly show continuous, mechanically clear transfer from the dropper to the skin. The dropper is held upright with its tip near the bottle opening in the earlier close views, then appears separated from the bottle as she raises it; the later cheek contact is shown in different pose. This makes the liquids path and the precise contact relationship diﬀicult to follow. The womans hand and arm movements otherwise look broadly plausible, and the frames do not establish definite structural deformation or impossible body motion. The concern is limited to the visible dropper-to-skin interaction, where continuity and contact are not convincingly demonstrated. Step 3 Main agent ocr_consistency[@ 4.0 s] Reasoning. The two preceding full-range checks leave the medias printed and displayed lettering as an important unresolved area. The scene contains several product packages and large background sign, and generated imagery often produces locally unstable or malformed glyphs even when the overall composition looks coherent. targeted OCR consistency check at 4.0 seconds is appropriate because the close-up composition makes the foreground bottle and nearby text more legible than in the opening wide view. This call should compare the apparent lettering across localized regions and determine whether any irregularity is confined to low-resolution text or affects prominent, readable labels. Such evidence is supporting rather than standalone proof: perspective, focus, motion, and stylized branding can reduce recognition quality. Nevertheless, high-confidence text anomaly in clear frame would materially strengthen the synthetic-media hypothesis when combined with the earlier temporal appearance and physical-continuity findings. Sub-agent returns. text suspicious (high). Issues: Malformed and irregularly branching strokes in the prominent bottle label; Fused strokes and unstable character boundaries across multiple smaller label lines; Structurally unresolved lettering on both foreground and background bottles. Reason: The supplied crops show repeated glyph-structure defects across separate text regions. The prominent label provides the clearest evidence, while the smaller lines and background label show additional supporting degradation. The assessment rests on visible stroke formation, not on the OCR strings or the wording they represent. 35 Step 4 Main agent: final verdict answer(fake) Verdict. The evidence converges on synthetic-media classification. The full-range visual inspection identifies persistent waxy, unusually smooth facial surface with crisp nearby details, which is medium-confidence appearance concern rather than an unmistakable boundary failure. The physical review independently finds medium-confidence issue in the dropper-to-cheek interaction: the sampled poses do not clearly establish continuous liquid transfer, although the broader hand and arm motion remains plausible. That limitation means the physical result is supportive, not decisive. The strongest evidence comes from the targeted text analysis at 4.0 seconds, which reports high-confidence malformed, fused, and structurally unresolved lettering across multiple foreground and background regions, including the prominent bottle label. These defects are not merely uncertain OCR readings; they concern visible glyph formation. Taken together, the repeated text irregularities, persistent rendered facial appearance, and unclear liquid contact outweigh the otherwise plausible staging and motion. The appropriate classification is fake. Figure 15 Garbled product label in generated cosmetics demonstration. Ground truth: fake; WeVisForensics prediction: fake; 5.0 s, silent. The appearance and physical sub-agents identify rendered facial surface and an unconvincing dropper-to-cheek liquid transfer, and the main agent targets the bottle with an OCR call at 4.0 s, which finds malformed strokes in the main label and fused characters in the smaller lines. On the 4.0 frame, colored boxes mark the PP-OCR text lines of the main label and the smaller lines, enlarged on the right. Investigation trace: cat at the wheel Step 1 Main agent common_sense[0.0--5.0 s] Reasoning. The sequence presents highly unusual staged-looking interaction: cat appears positioned at the steering wheel of small red car, while an oﬀicer stands beside it and police vehicle is behind them. Before assessing rendering artifacts, the first question is whether the depicted action is physically and semantically plausible. common-sense review across the full five-second interval can test whether the cats posture, apparent control of the vehicle, oﬀicers behavior, and vehicle motion form coherent real-world event. This broad temporal scope is useful because single frame could make an unusual but possible arrangement seem credible, whereas repeated frames may reveal whether the cat actually interacts with the controls or whether the scene remains frozen. The result should establish whether the central premise itself is credible, while leaving image-generation artifacts and text quality for separate checks. Sub-agent returns. issue (high). The scene presents cat as the apparent driver of full-size road car, seated upright behind the steering wheel and apparently operating it while police oﬀicer writes ticket beside the vehicle. The cats paws are placed on the wheel, but there is no visible human operator, restraint, or other mechanism that would make the cats control of the vehicle plausible. The oﬀicers ticketing behavior is coherent on its own, yet the central event depends on an animal performing human driving task without credible causal explanation. The car remains stationary in the sampled frames, so the anomaly is not based on an observed crash or impossible movement; it is the depicted affordance and action itself. The scene therefore conflicts with ordinary animal capabilities and vehicle operation. Step 2 Main agent visual_appearance[0.0--5.0 s] Reasoning. The preceding assessment identifies strong plausibility concern centered on the cats apparent role as driver, but that concern does not by itself distinguish deliberately staged scene from synthetic imagery. The next useful test is temporal visual consistency across the same complete interval. Comparing the cats face, paws, vehicle edges, oﬀicer, police car, and background can reveal whether details remain stable as the oﬀicer changes pose and the apparent vehicle motion progresses. Particular attention should go to fine boundaries and repeated structures, since generated imagery often preserves the broad composition while subtly regenerating local features between frames. This check can either provide independent support for an artificial origin or show that the unusual premise is visually coherent. It should remain focused on appearance continuity rather than re-evaluating the semantic plausibility already examined. 36 Sub-agent returns. issue (medium). The scene has conspicuously smooth, rendered appearance, most evident in the cats face and the oﬀicers exposed skin. Across the opening views, the cats forehead, cheeks, and muzzle have broad, softly blended fur shading with little fine strand detail, while its eyes and facial outline remain unusually clean and graphic. The oﬀicers cheek, forehead, and forearms similarly show smooth tonal transitions and simplified surface detail. This treatment contrasts with the more sharply delineated road texture, vehicle edges, and clothing outlines. The concern is the persistent synthetic softness of the subjects, rather than definite change in identity or lighting contradiction. The visible evidence supports an appearance anomaly with moderate confidence; it does not establish specific temporal flicker or particular facial feature changing shape. Step 3 Main agent ocr_consistency[@ 2.0 s] Reasoning. The two preceding checks leave the main question focused on whether the scenes visible text behaves like ordinary photographed signage. The license plate is prominent and contains short, high-contrast word, making it useful localized test: generated images often produce readable-looking lettering with unstable or malformed character boundaries, while genuine text may remain structurally consistent even when slightly blurred. Inspecting the plate at the specified two-second point is appropriate because it is clearly visible in the supplied chronology and can be evaluated independently of the cat-and-driver premise. This is narrow corroborating check, not standalone authenticity test. Its value depends on whether the lettering is legible and whether any irregularity is localized to the text rather than caused by general image softness, perspective, or compression. Sub-agent returns. text suspicious (medium). Issues: Localized background plate lettering is structurally unreadable and appears melted or unresolved; The clear foreground plate provides strong contrast with the degraded background plate text. Reason: One localized text region shows generation-like glyph dissolution and unstable character structure, while the other is regular and legible. Step 4 Main agent: final verdict answer(fake) Verdict. The evidence converges on synthetic or otherwise non-real depiction. The strongest finding is the high-confidence common-sense issue: the cat is presented as the apparent driver of road vehicle, with paws on the wheel but no credible mechanism explaining how it could operate the car. The oﬀicers ticketing behavior is coherent, but it does not resolve that central physical contradiction. Visual inspection adds moderate support, describing unusually smooth, rendered-looking fur and exposed skin, with simplified shading and clean graphic facial contours compared with sharper environmental details. The text check is also moderately suspicious: one localized plate region has melted or unresolved lettering, while another is clear, creating an inconsistent text-quality pattern. These appearance and text findings are not individually decisive, and the stationary vehicle limits motion-based inference, but together with the implausible central action they strongly favor an AI-generated scene. Therefore the media is fake. Figure 16 AI-generated traffic stop with cat at the wheel. Ground truth: fake; WeVisForensics prediction: fake; 5.0 s, silent. Commonsense and appearance sub-agents flag the cat-as-driver premise and rendered fur and skin, and an OCR call at 2.0 contrasts the legible foreground plate with the dissolved lettering on the background cruiser plate (enlarged on the right). 37 Investigation trace: real street recording Step 1 Main agent visual_appearance[0.0--8.3 s] Reasoning. The primary hypothesis is that this is genuine continuous street recording, but the repeated frames should first be checked for visual artifacts that could indicate synthetic generation. will examine the full available interval rather than single image, focusing on whether fixed structures, signage, barriers, vehicles, pedestrians, and the moving foreground subject retain stable geometry and appearance. This broad temporal scope is useful because generated media may reveal inconsistent textures, object boundaries, lighting, or background details even when individual frames look plausible. The foreground man and stroller deserve particular attention because their motion provides natural test of continuity, while the largely static street environment supplies reference for detecting unexplained changes. At this stage, the goal is to establish whether there are visible appearance anomalies; physical plausibility and text legibility can be assessed separately afterward. Sub-agent returns. no issue (medium). Across the sequence, the street scene retains consistent appearance: the storefront, road markings, barriers, buildings, trees, and parked vehicles keep their shapes, colors, and relative positions. The moving man and stroller remain visually coherent as they approach the left edge, with no clear boundary melting, duplication, or abrupt change in detail. Fine facial and clothing details are small, and the largely fixed viewpoint limits assessment of texture behavior under substantial motion or changing light. Within the visible regions, however, there is no distinct temporal appearance anomaly. Step 2 Main agent physical_consistency[0.0--8.3 s] Reasoning. The appearance review provides basis for treating the scene as visually stable, but it does not by itself establish that the observed motion follows ordinary physical relationships. The next question is whether the man, stroller, road obstacles, vehicles, and surrounding structures move consistently through time. will therefore inspect the same full interval with physical-consistency analysis. This scope is appropriate because it can test continuity of trajectories, contact with the pavement, object persistence, and possible distortions such as teleportation, merging, splitting, or implausible deformation. The scene appears to contain limited motion, so the analysis should distinguish absence of detected violations from strong evidence about dynamics that are not suﬀiciently exercised. In particular, the strollers path toward the frame edge and the parked or distant traﬀic should be compared against the fixed barriers, road markings, and buildings. This step can either add support for authenticity or identify concrete physical contradiction. Sub-agent returns. no issue (medium). The visible motion is physically coherent across the sampled frames. man pushes stroller along the sidewalk from the middle-left toward the left edge, with the stroller maintaining stable shape, orientation, and contact with the pavement. The child remains seated in the stroller, and the mans posture and hand placement are consistent with the movement. The stroller wheels stay aligned with the sidewalk, and there is no visible teleportation, sudden acceleration, limb distortion, object splitting, or implausible collision. The road barriers, parked vehicles, buildings, and other rigid structures remain fixed in place. The 2 FPS sampling does not show every intermediate movement, so very fine kinematic details cannot be checked, but the observed progression over the full sequence is natural and continuous enough to support no physical-consistency issue. Step 3 Main agent ocr_consistency[@ 4.0 s] Reasoning. The temporal and physical checks address motion and scene structure, while visible lettering remains an independent source of evidence. Synthetic imagery can produce unstable, malformed, or inconsistent text, especially on storefronts and road signs. will inspect the text at the supplied four-second point, where the main signage is clearly visible, using OCR consistency rather than attempting to infer meaning from the scene alone. The useful scope is localized: the large shop sign, speed marking, and nearby directional or warning text can be checked for coherent glyph shapes and ordinary perspective effects. This single-time inspection cannot establish temporal text stability across the entire clip, and small or blurred lettering may remain unresolved, so it should be treated as supporting evidence only. Combined with the earlier full-range checks, however, it can reveal whether prominent readable regions show the characteristic warping or incoherence often associated with generated imagery. Sub-agent returns. text ok (high). All supplied text regions show coherent glyph structure consistent with ordinary photographed signage. Minor softness and stylization are present but do not produce visible warping or generation-like text anomalies. 38 Step 4 Main agent: final verdict answer(real) Verdict. The full-range visual assessment found no distinct temporal appearance anomaly: the storefront, road markings, barriers, buildings, trees, and vehicles remain consistent, while the man and stroller retain coherent shapes and detail as they move. The physical-consistency assessment independently found natural, continuous motion, with stable stroller orientation, pavement contact, posture, and hand placement, and no observed teleportation, splitting, limb distortion, or implausible collision. Both findings are medium-confidence and the 2 FPS sampling leaves fine intermediate kinematics unresolved, so they are supportive rather than absolute. Its single-frame scope limits conclusions about text over time, but it provides no contradictory evidence.
